RESCA is a proposed disaster-response support platform for authorized emergency-service agencies, including police, ambulance, and fire services. It combines the presentation of available damage-assessment information with two-dimensional and three-dimensional area views, person-related assistance records, reported hazards, and response guidance. Through a website and mobile application, the project aims to help users understand an affected area, coordinate assistance, and maintain response-status information while retaining human responsibility for decisions.

Understanding disaster impacts and preparing for effective response are central concerns in disaster risk reduction. The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 identifies understanding disaster risk and strengthening preparedness for effective response among its priorities [1]. This context motivates the investigation of systems that help emergency organizations interpret and share relevant information.

Remote sensing offers one source of information about the physical effects of a disaster. Gupta et al. introduce xBD, a dataset containing pre-disaster and post-disaster satellite imagery, building annotations, and damage labels for research into change detection and building damage assessment [2]. This supports the investigation of image-based assessment as an input to situational awareness. It does not establish the accuracy or effectiveness of RESCA, which requires its own evaluation.

The proposed RESCA scenario also involves information that imagery alone cannot establish: people awaiting assistance, reported hazards, changing street conditions, and the status of a response. The motivation is to place these information types in a coherent spatial and case-based context. A user should be able to understand what a record represents, where it applies, and whether its information is current or requires confirmation.

Responsible handling of this information is part of the project motivation. OCHA describes data responsibility as the safe, ethical, and effective management of personal and non-personal data in humanitarian action, and notes that disclosure of sensitive data may cause harm [3]. RESCA therefore treats access to person-related information and the interpretation of uncertain observations as design concerns from the beginning.

The purpose of this Software Requirements Specification (SRS) introduction is to define the problem, intended audience, intended use, scope, terminology, and constraints of RESCA. It establishes a common foundation for the system description, detailed requirements, and design presented in the subsequent report sections.

Its objectives and boundaries provide a basis for deciding which capabilities belong to the proposal and for checking that later requirements and design decisions describe the same system. The success criteria identify observable outcomes to be used when planning verification.

RESCA is intended to support the review of a disaster-affected area by authorized emergency-service users. The website is envisaged as an environment for overview and coordination, while the mobile application supports relevant field interactions. Detailed user privileges are specified in the system-description and requirements sections.

A typical proposed use begins when incident-related information becomes available. This may include imagery used for damage assessment and separately supplied records concerning people, hazards, or response activities. An authorized user examines the area, selects a relevant record, reviews the information and its limitations, and records or coordinates the next action. Subsequent updates maintain the status of the assistance case.

Two-dimensional and three-dimensional views provide alternative spatial presentations where suitable data exist. Person tracking means following available person-related location or status updates within an authorized workflow. It does not establish continuous observation or automatic identification of people. Responder location and the location of a person requiring assistance are separate record types and must not be confused.

Route guidance is intended to help users interpret available movement options using relevant road and hazard information. The user remains responsible for assessing its suitability. A route is not a guarantee of current accessibility or safety. Similarly, image-derived damage information does not establish building occupancy, injury, or structural safety.

For the academic project, these activities are to be demonstrated through controlled scenarios and genuine preliminary evidence appropriate to the implementation stage. A demonstration does not establish readiness for operational emergency deployment.

RESCA addresses the problem of presenting different types of disaster-related information in a form that supports a shared understanding of the affected area. In the proposed scenario, damage observations, assistance needs, hazard reports, and response updates may originate from different sources and may refer to different times. Users must determine how these records relate geographically and which information is suitable for a decision.

Fragmented information can create specific difficulties in this scenario. A recorded assistance need may lack a verified location; an otherwise relevant street may have a newly reported obstruction; and a responder may not know whether another organization is already handling a case. The project investigates how spatial presentation and structured case updates can make these relationships visible. These are the problems defining the proposed use scenario, rather than claims that every emergency organization follows the same procedures.

The central project question is how to combine available assessment information and response records while preserving their source, update status, and uncertainty. The intended contribution is a coherent workflow for review and coordination. Demonstrating reduced response time or improved rescue outcomes would require a separate operational evaluation.

The proposed platform connects an assessment component with a response-support environment. Suitable before-and-after imagery can provide a basis for building-related damage predictions and visual summaries. These analytical outputs are presented alongside separately sourced person-related records, reported hazards, and response information. Their common spatial context helps the user examine relationships without treating one information type as proof of another.

The website and mobile application are intended to support the progression from viewing an incident area to reviewing a case, coordinating an action, and updating its status. Detailed technology choices and model architectures are addressed in later sections; this chapter defines their intended role and boundaries.

The project aim is to support situational awareness and assistance coordination through an understandable presentation of available disaster-related information. Table 1-2 expresses the objectives to which detailed requirements and verification activities should be linked.

Support coordination through defined user responsibilities and traceable response-status updates.

The proposal does not include autonomous dispatch, medical diagnosis, certified structural inspection, or guaranteed rescue outcomes. Detecting people beneath debris from ordinary RGB imagery is not a claimed capability. Geographic coverage and demonstration datasets are bounded by the data selected for evaluation.

Numerical acceptance thresholds and latency targets must be set before final acceptance testing, using the agreed dataset, hardware, and intended use. No accuracy or speed result is claimed in this chapter.

The proposed features address complementary information needs. Map views provide geographical context, damage layers present analytical observations, and hazard markers identify reported conditions that may affect access. Person-related records connect a possible assistance need with available location and review information.

Coordination features associate these records with permitted user actions and response-status updates. Route guidance supports movement decisions when suitable network information exists. Reports provide a readable summary of an assessment. Each feature must preserve the distinction between observed, predicted, and reviewed information.

This chapter reviews research relevant to the proposed RESCA workflow, from interpreting disaster imagery to sharing verified observations with response agencies. It examines what published methods can measure and what evidence is needed before those outputs inform an operational decision.

The review uses a targeted selection of studies. It started from Bela’s ranked list of 28 candidate papers and the seven detailed summaries, then checked the original papers and compared their methods with the project configurations. Appendix D records the candidate list and the papers carried into the review. Dataset papers and relevant workflow references provide context for the selected model studies.

The selection prioritises papers that explain a configured baseline, a proposed alternative, or an evaluation dataset. The comparisons distinguish findings from the source benchmarks, settings recorded in the repository, and evidence shown by the Project I prototype. The source list supports a focused review of this proposal.

The Sendai Framework emphasises understanding disaster risk [1]. The xBD dataset supplies paired satellite views and building damage annotations for studying post-disaster change [2]. A report or map can make these observations easier to review by showing the acquisition date, source, and status of each layer. In the proposed workflow, a change overlay directs attention to an area. An analyst then reviews the imagery and any corroborating evidence before assigning a damage status.

Fully convolutional networks (FCNs) showed how to train a model to produce a class map directly from an image [6]. U-Net uses an encoder and a decoder with skip connections that recover detail lost as features are downsampled [7]. These ideas underpin the configured building and damage masks. A mask can provide the footprint of an observation for a 2D map. A 3D view requires additional geometric or elevation information and a separate quality check.

Residual connections made deeper networks easier to train [8]. The building segmentation and Siamese change detection configurations use ResNet34 encoders. EfficientNet scales the depth, width, and image resolution together [9]. The repository uses EfficientNet-B3 in the six-channel before/after damage segmentation configuration and the four-class building-crop classifier. When comparing these baselines, the stacked image input and the crop input address different prediction tasks.

The original Transformer paper introduced an attention-based architecture for sequence modelling [10]. SegFormer applies a hierarchical Transformer encoder and a lightweight decoder to image segmentation [11]. The repository has SegFormer configurations for building masks, damage masks, and FloodNet. Performance on the source paper’s street-scene benchmarks does not establish performance on aerial disaster imagery.

DINOv3 uses self-supervised learning and Gram anchoring to preserve spatial features during training [12]. The authors provide satellite-pretrained variants. DINOv3 is a candidate for the building-crop comparison. The current classifier configuration freezes a DINOv2 backbone [13]. A controlled comparison would use the same labelled crops and data splits for the DINO-based classifiers and EfficientNet-B3.

The dataset and acquisition conditions also determine what the model can support. xBD provides paired satellite imagery with building damage annotations [2]. FloodNet provides annotated UAV imagery captured after Hurricane Harvey for flood-scene understanding [14]. Evaluations should report the data and metric for each task and test transfer to a separate event when suitable labelled data are available.
IDENTIFYING AND FOLLOWING PEOPLE WHO NEED ASSISTANCE

The ranked list identifies detector families for literature comparison. Existing aerial research in the report provides more direct application context. VisDrone covers detection and tracking in aerial sequences [15], and the land search-and-rescue study addresses people in aerial images [16]. ByteTrack uses lower-confidence detections to help associate objects between frames when observations are incomplete [17]. A tentative track can help a reviewer locate an observation across frames. The rescue workflow still needs an authorised reviewer to confirm an assistance case.

FloodNet provides a benchmark for recognising flooded surfaces in imagery [14]. Road-network routing uses the available network and edge costs to compare route options [18], [19]. A proposed route is therefore sensitive to stale road status and uncertain hazard locations. For RESCA, a mapped observation can support a review of a road segment. An operational restriction requires verified incident information and applicable agency rules.

The National Incident Management System describes common terminology and coordination across responding organisations [20]. Humanitarian data responsibility guidance provides a basis for access and handling decisions [3]. These sources inform two report requirements. Agencies need a shared view of verified incident updates, and records about assistance cases need access controls suited to the roles responsible for them.

The sources identify resources that support different parts of the proposed workflow. Maxar Open Data provides satellite imagery following selected disaster activations [21]. xBD and FloodNet provide labelled data for different research tasks [2], [14]. Table 2-1 compares the uses and scope of these resources. Their availability supports prototype research and evaluation. A market assessment would require separate evidence on operational tools, intended adopters, and deployment conditions.

RESCA is a proposed multi-agency platform for the hours and days after a disaster. Drones and, where available, satellites capture the affected area. The platform turns those images into one shared, georeferenced picture that Government, Police, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and Fire agencies can work from together. Six features carry the proposal. They are summarised in Table 3-3 and specified one by one in Section 3.2.1.
Before/After Damage Assessment and Restoration Cost
A damage grade for every building and an indicative low–high cost to restore it.
One georeferenced map in 2D and 3D, and routes that avoid blocked or flooded roads for the chosen vehicle.
Aerial Person Detection under Partial Visibility
Candidate locations of people seen from the drone, including people of whom only the head or limbs are visible.
Multi-Object Person Tracking and Assistance Cases
The same person followed across images, and a managed case from first sighting to rescue.
A warning, no-entry zone and road closure when floodwater lies near an energised power line.
Frozen, approved and shareable situation, damage, casualty and after-action reports.

The functional requirements are grouped by feature. Two groups that all features depend on come first: access and incident participation, and imagery intake. They are followed by the six features F1 to F6 and by the field and citizen functions that feed them. Each group opens with a description of the feature and the reasons behind its requirements.

RESCA is used by several agencies at once, so the first group of requirements settles who may see what. Every user belongs to one agency (Government, Police, EMS or Fire) and holds one of four roles that mean the same thing in every agency. The Platform Administrator sits above all agencies. A disaster is represented by one shared incident. The lead agency opens it and invites the others, and an agency sees incident data only while its participation is active. Inside the incident, each agency runs its own missions and assigns them to a team or to a single responder. One responder serves in one team at a time, following the unity-of-command principle of the Incident Command System [20].

All six features start from images. A capture session groups the images of one flight or one satellite pass and is labelled as pre-event or post-event; this label is the before/after axis that F1 depends on. The platform checks each upload for duplicates and for usable location metadata, stitches post-event drone photos into an orthomosaic, and runs the AI models as tracked processing jobs. Every AI result keeps a link to the model version and the input images that produced it, so a reviewer can always answer the question “where did this number come from?”.

3.2.1.3 Feature F1: Before/After Damage Assessment and Restoration Cost

After an earthquake, flood or storm, decision makers need two answers quickly: which buildings are damaged, and roughly what it will cost to restore them. F1 answers both at the level of a single building. Building footprints come from open map sources (OpenStreetMap or Overture), from AI extraction, or from manual entry. Where pre-event and post-event imagery both cover a building, the model compares them; where only post-event imagery exists, it assesses the post-event image alone and the result is labelled accordingly so users can weigh it.

Each assessed building receives one of the four grades of the xBD damage scale: No Damage, Minor Damage, Major Damage or Destroyed [2]. The model also reports a probability for each grade, so an Analyst can see the difference between a confident “Destroyed” and a borderline one. An Analyst or a field team may confirm or correct the grade. The platform keeps every assessment of a building as history and treats exactly one as current.

The indicative restoration cost follows the repair-ratio idea used in the FEMA Hazus methodology [23]. For a building with footprint area A and n floors, the floor area is A × n. The cost range is this floor area multiplied by the repair ratio for its damage grade and by the local unit cost per square metre for its occupancy and construction type. Both the ratio and the unit cost have a low and a high value, which gives a low–high range instead of a single figure that would suggest false precision. The unit costs and ratios live in editable cost profiles per region and currency. Once a cost estimate is published it is kept as a snapshot, so a report never changes silently when an assumption is later edited. The estimate supports planning and prioritisation; it is not an engineering survey or an insurance valuation.

3.2.1.4 Feature F2: 2D/3D Mapping and Rescue Route Planning

F2 gives every agency the same picture of the ground. The stitched orthomosaic is shown over a base map in 2D, and a 3D city view is built from the same drone imagery (surface and terrain models and a 3D mesh). Both views show the same layers: buildings, hazards, people, zones and routes. A user who selects a building in 2D still has it selected after switching to 3D.

Roads are held as a network of segments, each with a current condition: clear, debris, flooded, blocked or closed by a hazard. A condition may come from AI analysis, from a responder on the ground or from a verified citizen report, and the source is kept. Route planning then works for a specific vehicle. A four-wheel-drive rescue truck may cross shallow water that an ambulance must avoid, so each vehicle carries a maximum safe water depth. The planner uses shortest-path search, Dijkstra or A* [18], on the road network [19]. Closed segments, and flooded segments deeper than the vehicle can cross, are excluded. 3.2.1.5 Feature F3: Aerial Person Detection under Partial Visibility

Seen from a drone, people look very different from the upright figures in everyday photographs. They are small, viewed from above or at an angle, and in a disaster they are often partly hidden by debris, water, vegetation or a roof edge. Public aerial benchmarks such as VisDrone [15] and search-and-rescue studies such as HERIDAL [16] show how much harder detection becomes under these conditions. F3 is specified for this setting. A detection is required even when only a head or limbs are visible. The result says how much of the person was visible: full, partial, head only or limbs only, with an estimated occlusion ratio and, where the image allows, a posture.

A detection is useful to a rescue team only if it can be found on the ground. The platform therefore converts each image position into a map position and attaches an uncertainty radius in metres. The radius grows with coarser ground resolution and weaker GPS accuracy. Images taken from too high to resolve a person are not analysed, and the Analyst is told why. Thermal images are processed when the drone supplies them. Two limits of scope are stated explicitly. F3 covers people who are at least partly visible from the air, not people buried under rubble. Every detection is a candidate for a human to review, not a confirmed person.

3.2.1.6 Feature F4: Multi-Object Person Tracking and Assistance Cases

F4 turns isolated sightings into information a commander can act on, in three levels. A detection is one sighting in one image. A track links detections of the same person across consecutive frames or overlapping images and gives that person a stable identifier, in the manner of modern multi-object trackers such as ByteTrack [17]. An assistance case is a person, or a group, that a human has decided needs help. Each track keeps its path, last known position, time last seen and a movement state of moving or stationary. A person who stays still while the area around them changes may be injured or trapped, so stationary tracks are brought forward for review.

Assistance cases do not come from the drone alone. A verified citizen request or a responder’s report creates a case in the same list, so a commander works from one queue whatever the source. Cases are triaged with the four START categories, Immediate (red), Delayed (yellow), Minor (green) and Expectant (black) [24]. A case moves from detection to rescue, can be linked to the building where people may be trapped and to the hospital or shelter receiving them, and keeps a timestamped event history. Because a track describes the past, the platform always shows how old its last position is.

3.2.1.7 Feature F5: Compound Hazard Alerts (“Electrified Water”)

Disasters rarely produce one danger at a time. Floodwater is dangerous, and so is a fallen power line. A street flooded next to a line that is still energised can kill a responder who wades through it, even though neither hazard alone would have stopped the team. F5 watches for such combinations. The platform keeps two kinds of record: hazards (flood, fire, gas leak and structural collapse), reported by AI, responders or citizens; and infrastructure assets (power lines, transformers and gas pipelines) with a power state that the utility or an authorised user keeps current.

A rule engine compares the two. Its first rule is named Electrified Water. It fires when an active flood hazard lies within the configured rule distance of a power line or transformer that has not been confirmed de-energised. The rule and buffer distances require confirmation with civil-defence and utility guidance before operational use. When the rule fires, the platform does four things in one step. It draws a buffered danger zone and shows it as a no-entry zone. It closes every road segment inside that zone. It marks active routes through those roads as invalid and offers new ones. It warns the assigned teams and every responder whose last position is in or near the zone. An asset whose power state is unknown is treated as energised. When the utility confirms the line is off and a Commander resolves the alert, the roads it closed reopen, unless another active alert still closes them. Rules are stored as data, so further combinations, such as a gas leak near a fire, can be added later without changing the program.

This section describes how the proposed RESCA platform is organised to meet the requirements in Section 3.2. It covers the System Analysis and Design topics listed in the Project I guide [4]: architecture, design rationale, database and file design, user interface design, class, sequence and use case diagrams, and the detailed design of the parts that carry the most risk. Each figure is linked to the requirement and use-case identifiers of Section 3.2, and Table 3-48 at the end of the section collects those links. The design is a proposal. Diagrams describe intended behaviour, and the screen illustrations in Section 3.3.4 are design illustrations, not screenshots of working software; the evidence produced so far is reported in Chapter 4.

Two sources of notation are used throughout. Structural and behavioural diagrams follow the Unified Modeling Language (UML) 2.5.1 [27]. The architecture is described through several views (context, logical and deployment), in the manner of ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 [28], because no single diagram can show both what the platform does and where it runs.

Figure 3-2 places RESCA among the people and services it depends on. Staff of the four agency types (Government, Police, EMS and Fire) use the web command console. Two choices about volume complete the physical design. Every geometry column has a spatial index, and the two tables that grow fastest, responder positions and the audit log, are divided into monthly partitions. Old months can then be archived or deleted as whole units when the retention period ends (NFR-PV-04), without slowing the current month.

Decision D-04 places access control in the database. The design uses PostgreSQL row-level security [29]: every one of the 56 tables has security enabled and denies access by default, and policies then open exactly the rows each kind of user may see. Applications never connect as the owner of the schema. Instead, each connects through one of the four group roles in Table 3-43.
Table 3-43: Database roles and what they may access
The application interface, acting for a signed-in agency user.
Rows allowed by the policies for that user's agency, role and incident participation.
All operational rows; it acts for the platform, not for a user.

At the start of each request, the application interface records the identifier of the signed-in user for the duration of that transaction only, so a pooled connection cannot carry one user's identity into another user's request. Every policy derives the user's agency, role and permissions from that identifier at the time of the request. A suspended user therefore loses access on the next request, and an agency loses access to an incident as soon as its participation is withdrawn (FR-AC-05, NFR-PV-02). Draft reports remain visible only inside the authoring agency until they are approved or shared (FR-RP-04, FR-RP-06).

Policies decide which rows a user may change; column guards decide which fields. A field responder may change the status of a mission they are assigned to but not its target or priority, and users may edit their own name and phone number but not their role or agency. Password hashes cannot be read by any application role; sign-in uses a single protected function. Inserts, updates and deletes on 27 operational tables are written to the audit log with the acting user and the values before and after the change (NFR-SC-05), and no application role can modify the log (NFR-SC-06). The demonstration uses a single urban crop and two dates separated by about seven months. Differences in lighting, viewing geometry, image alignment, intervening land use, and post-event activity can influence the pixel-change layer. Its marks require human interpretation and independent labels before they can support a damage claim.

The available outputs provide visual evidence only. They contain no measured detection accuracy or user evaluation. They cannot establish structural safety, occupancy, casualty status, or road passability. The current demonstration also provides no basis for live dispatch or route selection.

The next step is to compare the pixel-change baseline with a documented damage-assessment method using labelled data. The report should record the evaluation split, class definitions, and metrics before drawing conclusions about accuracy. A SWOT analysis sets out the internal strengths and weaknesses of the proposed platform next to the external opportunities and threats in the environment where it would be used. Strengths and weaknesses describe RESCA itself: its features, data and design choices. Opportunities and threats describe things the team does not control, such as regulation, partner agencies, networks and public expectations. Figure C-1 summarises the analysis, and the paragraphs that follow explain each quadrant. Table C-1 then shows how the requirements in Chapter 3 respond to the weaknesses and threats.

The main strength of RESCA is that it brings work that is usually spread across separate tools into one shared incident. Government, Police, EMS and Fire teams see the same map, the same people who may need help and the same hazards. Every AI result keeps a link to the model version and the images that produced it (FR-IM-07), so a commander can check where a number came from before acting on it. The platform also joins features that support one another. Building-damage information helps prioritise locations for review. Verified assistance cases can become route destinations, and confirmed hazards can restrict road access. Person detection is specified for partly visible people and always reports a position uncertainty in metres. Routing takes into account the vehicle and the depth of floodwater. Hazard rules and cost profiles are stored as data, so they can be adapted to a new region without rewriting the program. Finally, the intended open-source geospatial stack keeps licence costs low for public agencies.

The quality of every AI layer depends on its training data. Public aerial disaster datasets exist [2], [15], but they cover a limited range of building styles, regions and image conditions. The models may therefore perform worse on local buildings than published results suggest. Aerial imagery cannot show people under rubble or inside buildings; the platform states this limit rather than hiding it. Cost estimates are only as good as the local unit costs entered in the cost profiles, and those figures still have to be collected. The platform needs drones, flying weather and some network connection to work at full capacity. Its analysis is also computationally heavy. Stitching an orthomosaic, building a 3D model and running detection, damage and tracking models over hundreds of high-resolution images need powerful graphics processors (GPUs) and large memory. Without that hardware, or affordable cloud capacity, results arrive more slowly, just when speed matters most. The Electrified Water rule depends on knowing whether a line is energised, which requires cooperation from the utility. Lastly, the platform is a proposal. It has not yet been evaluated with real response agencies.

Civil-defence and emergency services increasingly use drones, which creates a natural place for a platform that turns their images into decisions. Open map data (OpenStreetMap, Overture) and open datasets and models lower the cost of building and testing such a platform. Floods and earthquakes in the region keep the need visible. There is room to partner with civil defence for realistic scenarios, with universities for annotated data, and with utilities for power-state information. Because hazard rules are data, new combinations such as a gas leak near a fire can be added later. Historical incidents stored in the platform could also support training exercises and post-event learning.

Drone flights need permits and are limited by airspace rules, which may delay or prevent imaging at the moment it is most needed. Aerial images of people raise privacy and legal questions, and public trust could suffer if the data were misused. There is also a risk that users trust the AI too much: a missed person or a false alarm in a rescue setting has real consequences. Networks are often damaged in a disaster area. Agencies may be reluctant to share data with each other or to change established ways of working. As a public-safety system, the platform would also be an attractive target for cyber attacks.
